title: Judah Halevi
hook: poet who wrote that his heart was in the east while he lived at the end of the west

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Gabirol's royal crown. Your line was the royal crown. Today, a poet whose heart lived somewhere else.

A phone sits on a kitchen table in one city, open to the weather in another. Some people keep an app like that: the forecast for where their parents were born, or where someone they love lives now. They check it without thinking. Rain there. Sun there. The body is here, and part of the attention is always there. A poet in medieval Spain put something like that split into a short Hebrew poem. Today, Judah Halevi, the poet of the heart that faced east.
screen: `THE WEATHER IN ANOTHER CITY.` → `BODY HERE, ATTENTION THERE.` → `A POET WHOSE HEART FACED EAST.`

segments.voice: Judah Halevi lived in Christian and Muslim Spain: a doctor by trade, a celebrated poet, with friends, students and a comfortable life. And yet one short poem of his opens with a split. Put plainly: my heart is in the east, and I am at the far end of the west. East is Jerusalem, the land of Israel. West is Spain, the edge of the map as he knew it. He asks how he can taste food or enjoy anything while Zion is in other hands and he is far away. Leaving all the good things of Spain would be easy, he says, if only he could see the dust of the ruined sanctuary. That longing has deep roots. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven, sung by exiles by the rivers of Babylon, says in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Halevi makes that old vow personal and present tense. He also wrote a set of poems to Zion itself, addressing the land like a beloved; some of them are recited on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple's destruction. Here is what lifts it beyond a poem. He decided to go. His poems describe the sea voyage, the waves, the fear, the ship. Tradition tells a legend that he reached the gates of Jerusalem, knelt to kiss the ground while reciting his poem to Zion, and was struck down by a passing rider. Nobody can confirm that story. But the poems that survive show a man who did not only long. He packed.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE LIFE IN SPAIN.` · `MY HEART IS IN THE EAST.` · then, large: `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `HE DID NOT ONLY LONG. HE WENT.`

segments.voice: Feel where your body is, the chair, the floor, and then ask gently where your heart is right now: with a person, a place, a worry, a hope. Don't judge it; let it point, and stay with that direction for a few breaths. If you pray, you can bring that place or person into your prayer in your own words.
Judah Halevi. A poet and doctor in Spain who wrote that his heart was in the east, wrote poems to Zion, and set out to go there. Today's word.
Your line: my heart in the east. A longing that ended up as a journey. Day nine hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Judah Halevi's poems to Zion are part of the kinot, the laments recited on Tisha B'Av in some communities, and his line about the heart in the east is quoted in Jewish writing about the land of Israel.

chat.says: Halevi had a good life in Spain. Why did his poems keep pining for Jerusalem?
options: His heart was in the east, in Zion, and in the end he set out to go.
He was forced out of Spain, so his poems mourn the home he lost.
He wrote of Jerusalem only as a symbol and never meant to travel.
chat.meaning: His poem says my heart is in the east; he wrote odes to Zion, and his poems describe the voyage he took.
